11	Cock PJ, Antao T, Chang JT, Chapman BA, Cox CJ, Dalke A, Friedberg I,

16	
17	> SUMMARY: The Biopython project is a mature open source international
18	> collaboration of volunteer developers, providing Python libraries for a
19	> wide range of bioinformatics problems. Biopython includes modules for
20	> reading and writing different sequence file formats and multiple sequence
21	> alignments, dealing with 3D macro molecular structures, interacting with
22	> common tools such as BLAST, ClustalW and EMBOSS, accessing key online
23	> databases, as well as providing numerical methods for statistical

26	## 2. The sequence feature model (Biopython Tutorial, chapter "Sequence annotation")
27	
28	The Biopython `SeqFeature` class describes a region on a parent sequence
29	(typically a `SeqRecord`). The design is heavily based on the GenBank/EMBL
30	feature tables. Key attributes:
31	
32	- `type` — a textual description of the kind of feature (for instance
33	  `CDS` or `gene`).
34	- `location` — the location of the feature on the sequence, delegated to a
35	  location object (see below).
36	- `strand` — shorthand for `location.strand`, the strand on the sequence
37	  that the feature is located on. For double stranded nucleotide sequence
38	  this may be `1` for the top strand, `-1` for the bottom strand, `0` if
39	  the strand is important but unknown, or `None` if it doesn't matter. This
40	  is `None` for proteins, or single stranded sequences.
41	- `qualifiers` — a Python dictionary of additional information about the
42	  feature, mirroring the qualifiers in GenBank/EMBL feature tables.

44	### 2.1 Positions and locations
45	
46	- A *position* refers to a single position on a sequence, which may be
47	  fuzzy or not (for instance `5`, `20`, `<100` and `>200`).
48	- A *location* is a region of sequence bounded by positions, for instance
49	  `5..20`.
50	
51	Most feature locations are simple: a start coordinate, an end coordinate,
52	and a strand — the `SimpleLocation` object. Complex locations made up of
53	several regions are represented by the `CompoundLocation` object, whose
54	main usage is handling `join` locations in EMBL/GenBank files.
55	
56	Biopython locations follow the Python counting convention: zero-based,
57	half-open intervals. A `SimpleLocation(5, 18)` covers the same bases as the
58	1-based inclusive GenBank notation `6..18`.
59	
60	### 2.2 Sequence described by a feature or location
61	
62	A `SeqFeature` or location object does not directly contain a sequence;
63	the location describes how to obtain it from the parent sequence. The
64	`extract` method handles strand and compound structure:
65	
66	```python
67	>>> from Bio.Seq import Seq
68	>>> from Bio.SeqFeature import SeqFeature, SimpleLocation
69	>>> seq = Seq("ACCGAGACGGCAAAGGCTAGCATAGGTATGAGACTTCCTTCCTGCCAGTGCTGAGGAACTGGGAGCCTAC")
70	>>> feature = SeqFeature(SimpleLocation(5, 18, strand=-1), type="gene")
71	>>> feature_seq = feature.extract(seq)
72	>>> print(feature_seq)
73	AGCCTTTGCCGTC
74	```
75	
76	For a minus-strand feature this equals slicing the parent sequence and
77	taking the reverse complement. Gene and CDS features defined with joins are
78	the union of their parts — they do not cover any introns. The length of a
79	`CompoundLocation` is the sum of the lengths of its constituent regions.
80	
81	### 2.3 Reverse-complementing SeqRecord objects
82	
83	The `SeqRecord` object's `reverse_complement` method reverse-complements
84	the sequence, and **any features are transferred with the location and
85	strand recalculated**. Per-letter annotation is copied but reversed. Most
86	record-level annotation is *not* transferred by default: the record id,
87	name, description, annotations, and database cross references are dropped
88	unless explicitly requested, because they refer to the original sequence.
89	In particular, when exporting a reverse-complemented record to GenBank you
90	must set `molecule_type` in the annotations again.
91	
92	### 2.4 Circular sequences and shifting the origin
93	
94	For a circular genome, the tutorial demonstrates shifting the origin by
95	slicing and re-joining the record:
96	
97	```python
98	>>> shifted = record[2000:] + record[:2000]
99	```
100	
101	The coordinates of features are recalculated under such transformations;
102	features may end up split across the new sequence ends, and circular
103	records can therefore legitimately carry features whose location consists
104	of one region near the end of the sequence joined with a region near the
105	start.
106	
107	## 3. The INSDC Feature Table Definition (GenBank/EMBL/DDBJ location syntax)
108	
109	Excerpted from the DDBJ/EMBL/GenBank Feature Table Definition
110	(<https://www.insdc.org/submitting-standards/feature-table/>), sections
111	3.4 "Location" and 5 "Examples of sequence annotation".
112	
113	### 3.1 Purpose and conventions
114	
115	The location indicates the region of the presented sequence which
116	corresponds to a feature. The location contains at least one sequence
117	location descriptor and may contain one or more operators with one or more
118	sequence location descriptors. Base numbers refer to the numbering in the
119	entry; this numbering designates the first base (5' end) of the presented
120	sequence as base 1, and spans are inclusive (`12..78` includes the ending
121	base).
122	
123	A site between two adjoining nucleotides, such as an endonucleolytic
124	cleavage site, is indicated by listing the two points separated by a carat
125	(`^`). The permitted formats for this descriptor are `n^n+1` (for example
126	`55^56`), or, **for circular molecules, `n^1`, where `n` is the full length
127	of the molecule**, i.e. `1000^1` for a circular molecule of length 1000 —
128	a site that wraps across the sequence origin.
129	
130	### 3.2 Operators
131	
132	The location operator is a prefix that specifies what must be done to the
133	indicated sequence to find or construct the location corresponding to the
134	feature:
135	
136	- `complement(location)` — Find the complement of the presented sequence
137	  in the span specified by "location" (i.e., read the complement of the
138	  presented strand in its 5'-to-3' direction).
139	- `join(location,location, ... location)` — The indicated elements should
140	  be joined (placed end-to-end) to form one contiguous sequence.
141	- `order(location,location, ... location)` — The elements can be found in
142	  the specified order (5' to 3' direction), but nothing is implied about
143	  the reasonableness about joining them.
144	
145	The operator `complement` can be used in combination with either `join` or
146	`order`. A location written **without** any `complement()` operator
147	describes a feature on the presented strand of the sequence.
148	
149	### 3.3 Location examples from the specification
150	
151	```text
152	467               Points to a single base in the presented sequence
153	340..565          Points to a continuous range of bases
154	join(12..78,134..202)
155	                  Regions 12 to 78 and 134 to 202 should be joined to form
156	                  one contiguous sequence
157	complement(34..126)
158	                  Start at the base complementary to 126 and finish at the
159	                  base complementary to base 34 (the feature is on the
160	                  strand complementary to the presented strand)
161	complement(join(2691..4571,4918..5163))
162	                  Joins regions 2691 to 4571 and 4918 to 5163, then
163	                  complements the joined segments (the feature is on the
164	                  strand complementary to the presented strand)
165	join(complement(4918..5163),complement(2691..4571))
166	                  Complements regions 4918 to 5163 and 2691 to 4571, then
167	                  joins the complemented segments (the feature is on the
168	                  strand complementary to the presented strand)
169	```
170	
171	### 3.4 A circular molecule example
172	
173	The specification's example for an artificial cloning vector (a circular
174	molecule of 5300 bp) includes a feature that crosses the sequence origin,
175	written as a join of a region at the start of the sequence with a region
176	near its end:
177	
178	```text
179	     source        1..5300
180	                   /organism="Cloning vector pABC"
181	     CDS           join(complement(1..799),complement(5080..5120))
182	                   /gene="mob1"
183	                   /product="mobilization protein 1"
184	```
